paragraphs.text: Heb., Tsor, whence came Tyre. It was the chief city of Phoenicia, the chief market of the East, a very microcosm or epitome of the whole world, for its wealth and wickedness. It was not far from Judea - our Saviour {Mat 15:21} went from Galilee into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon - in whose misery she made herself merry, {Eze 26:2} and is therefore here threatened with utter destruction.
i.e., Of Tartessus, in Spain, or of Tarsus, in Cilicia, St Paul’s country, or of the main ocean.
viz., By Nebuchadnezzar, and afterwards by Alexander the Great, who of an island made it part of the continent, and then razed it to the ground. {a}
Or thus: So that there is no house, nor coming in for those from Chittim, is made known to them.
paragraphs.anchor: So that there is no house.

paragraphs.text: {a} Plin., lib. v. cap. 19.
A nundinatorio strepitu quiescite, et plorate, Be quiet, and mourn.
paragraphs.anchor: Be still, ye inhabitants of the isle.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Of Nile, by the overflowing whereof Egypt is made exceeding fertile, being styled the "granary of the world." Tyre was much enriched by its store thereto transported through the midland sea, called here great waters.
paragraphs.anchor: And by great waters the seed of Sihor

paragraphs.text: sc., Of Tyre, thy daughter and confederate.
Or, The seaport. By the sea and seaport we are to understand Tyre, who sat in the sea, as now Venice doth, and sovereigned it.
paragraphs.anchor: For the sea hath spoken, even the strength of the sea.

paragraphs.text: I send forth no colonies, as sometimes I have done. Pliny saith of Tyre, Olim partu clara urbibus genitis, Lepti, Utica, Carthagine, etiam Gadibus extra orbem conditis. {a} But now it was past that time of day with her.
paragraphs.anchor: I travail not, nor bring forth children.

paragraphs.text: {a} Plin., lib. v. cap. 19.
i.e, Concerning their overthrow once at the Red Sea. {Exo 15:14} They are also shortly to be overrun by Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God hath promised Egypt, as his pay for his pains taken in taking Tyre.
paragraphs.anchor: As at the report concerning Egypt

paragraphs.text: Tyrii migrate coloni, be packing any whither, and make any shift to save your lives, Ultra Sauromatas fugite hinc, &c. To Carthage many of them went, say some; and the Septuagint; for ships of Tarshish {Isa 23:1} have ships of Carthage.

q.d., So ye were wont to hold her, and to boast of her; but now it is somewhat otherwise. Cities die as well as men, {a} saith one. They also have their times and their turns, their rise and their ruin. Hic immoremur parum et pedem figamus oportet. Let this be duly considered, and an "abiding city" sought. {Heb 12:14} The wicked may revel in this world, the godly only rejoice.
Palaetyre, or the old town especially: and this was a piece of her silly glory;
paragraphs.anchor: Whose antiquity is of ancient days.

paragraphs.text: “ Urbs fur ills Tyros priscis quae condita saeclis,
Innumerosque suo repetens ab Agenore soles,
Aeternos demens spe praesumebat honores. ”
{a} ’Lποθνησκουσι και αι πολεις ωσπες οι ανθρωποι.
Heb., The crowning or crowned: a city of kings, {a} as Cyneas once said of Rome, This is a style better befitting heaven and the crowned saints there.
Little kings, as we say. So they are at Venice; so the Hogens Moghens of the Netherlands.
{a} Vidi civitatem regum. See the state of kings.
Here the prophet sets forth both who had decreed the downfall of this famous and flourishing city; and why? See Eze 27:5-7.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord of hosts hath purposed it.

paragraphs.text: Ut faedet fastum omnis gloriae; to bring down the height of all haughtiness. This hath God Almighty decreed, and it shall stand. "Let us, therefore, have grace, whereby we may serve him with reverence and godly fear." {Heb 12:28}
paragraphs.anchor: To stain the pride of all glory.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Hastily: {a} Abi praeceps, pack up and begone with all speed, be there never so many of you here at Tyre.
paragraphs.anchor: Pass through the land as a river

paragraphs.text: Heb., Girdle - that is, soldiery, or shipping, or sea to encompass it. Oecolampadius sets this sense upon the words, Non est ei cingulum reliquum, There is not so much as a girdle or such like lowly commodity left in Tyre, she had been so plundered.
{a} Indefinenter et cito. - Jun.

That "mighty hand" of his, {1Pe 5:6} wherewith he spanneth the heavens, {Isa 48:13} brought the Red Sea upon the Egyptians, {Exo 14:26} and still shaketh the wicked out of the earth, as by a canvas. {Job 38:13}
Shook and shattered them - viz., by Nebuchadnezzar; the kingdom of Tyre especially, to the terror of others. {Eze 26:15}
"That man of war." {Exo 15:3} "Mighty in battle." {Psa 24:8}
Bidding his forces fall on.
Heb., Against, or concerning, Canaan; so he calleth Tyre the posterity of the old Canaanites, and a place of great merchandise. See Hos 12:7.
Heb., Exult, revel.
Or, Ravished damsel, daughter of Zidon, hactenus intacta vi hostili, never till now subdued.
Asyndeton, q.d., Haste, haste.
To Cyprus, Greece, Italy.
Safety or shelter. Cain’s curse was upon them; the visible vengeance of God followed them close at heels. See Deu 28:65-66.
paragraphs.anchor: There also shalt thou have no rest.

paragraphs.text: q.d., The Chaldees were once no such considerable people, but lay hid under the grandeur of the Assyrian monarchy, which did set them up. Howbeit in time the Assyrians at length were devoured by the Chaldees, Nineveh by Babylon; Filia devoravit matrem, as the proverb is. And why may not the like be done to Tyre? Others make this to be the prophet’s speech to the Chaldees, Behold, O land of the Chaldees! This people, of Tyre, was not, however they boast of their antiquity, till the Assyrians, those monarchs of the world, founded it, Ut esset statio carinis, to be a fit place for shipping, or for barbarians. See 2Ki 17:24. Down with it, therefore; bring it to vastity. {a}
paragraphs.anchor: Behold the land of the Chaldeans

paragraphs.text: {a} Calvin.

He concludeth this prophecy of Tyre’s downfall as he began. {Isa 23:1} The inhabitants of Tarshish, or Tarsus in Cilicia, were great ship masters; they sent a navy of a hundred ships to Xerxes when he went against Greece.
i.e., Laid aside by God, as if not at all minded in her misery: slighted also and unfrequented by men, as a withered harlot.
So long as the Jews, whom they jeered, were held captives in Babylon.
i.e., The duration of the Babylonish monarchy, under Nebuchadnezzar, his son, and his son’s son. {Jer 27:7}
paragraphs.anchor: According to the days of one king

paragraphs.text: Ut meretrix, i.e., Mercatrix. Harlots fallen into some foul disease are abandoned; but recovering thereof, they seek, by singing and other allurements, to regain their paramours; so should Tyre deal by her old customers, being, as was once said of Helena after her return from Troy, ηη παλαι γυνη, no changeling, but as good as ever.
paragraphs.anchor: Shall Tyre sing as an harlot.

paragraphs.text: In bidding her do so, he foretelleth that she shall do so - sc., ad ingenium suum redire, fall to her former practices.
The Tyrians were much addicted to music. {Eze 26:13; Eze 28:13}

Bad though she be, he will graciously visit her, both by suffering her to grow rich again, as here, and by converting some of them to the faith of Christ. {Isa 23:18} See it fulfilled, Act 21:3-5. Eusebius also telleth of many made martyrs there.
Being once converted, they shall leave heaping and hoarding wealth, and find other use for it - viz., to feed and clothe God’s ministers and poor people freely and largely.
The Vulgate hath it Vestientur ad vetustatem.
